sources.title: UCL Module Catalogue 2026/27: MATH0009 Newtonian Mechanics

about: Newtonian Mechanics is a 15-credit Term 2 module for first-year UCL Mathematics students, following on from Applied Mathematics (MATH0008) and Mathematical Methods 1 (MATH0010). The 2026–27 syllabus covers forces, moments and couples, Newton's laws and conservation laws, motion with one degree of freedom, vector differential equations, plane polar coordinates with central forces, conics, Kepler's laws and stability, then examples from cylindrical geometry and systems with transfer of mass. Vector methods, including vector differential equations, are used extensively. Assessment is 85% examination and 15% coursework, and you need at least 40% in the exam as well as overall to pass.
topics: Newton's laws, momentum, angular momentum and energy
Particle motion with one degree of freedom
Plane polar coordinates and central forces

notes.body:
The module starts by treating force as a vector with a point of application, and by measuring its turning effect with the cross product. Throughout, r is a position vector from a chosen origin O, and i, j, k are the usual right-handed unit vectors.

Force and moment
- A force F acting at a point with position r has moment (torque) about O given by G = r × F. Its direction is the axis of rotation it tends to produce (right-hand rule); its magnitude is |F| times the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action.
- Sliding F along its line of action does not change its moment: if r is replaced by r + sF then (r + sF) × F = r × F.
- Changing the reference point: the total moment about a point A (position a) of forces Fᵢ at rᵢ is G_A = Σ (rᵢ − a) × Fᵢ = G_O − a × R, where R = Σ Fᵢ is the resultant.
- Order matters: r × F = −F × r. Writing F × r is the most common sign error.

Example. F = (1, 2, 0) N acts at r = (3, 0, 0) m. Then G = r × F = (0, 0, 6) N m: an anticlockwise turning effect about the z-axis. Check: |F| = √5 and the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action is 6/√5, whose product is 6.

Couples
- A couple is a pair of forces F and −F acting along different parallel lines. Its resultant is zero, but its moment is not.
- If they act at r₁ and r₂, the moment is r₁ × F + r₂ × (−F) = (r₁ − r₂) × F, which does not depend on O. A couple therefore has the same moment about every point.
- Example: (0, 5, 0) N at (2, 0, 0) and (0, −5, 0) N at (−2, 0, 0) give total moment (0, 0, 20) N m about any point.

Reduction of a force system. Any system of forces on a rigid body is equivalent to a single force R acting at a chosen point A together with a couple of moment G_A. Two systems are equivalent when they have the same resultant and the same moment about one (hence every) point.

Equilibrium of a rigid body
- Conditions: Σ Fᵢ = 0 and Σ rᵢ × Fᵢ = 0 (moments about any one point). In two dimensions this gives three scalar equations.
- Choose the point for taking moments to eliminate unknown forces.
- Friction: at a rough contact the friction F and normal reaction N satisfy |F| ≤ μN, with equality in limiting equilibrium. A smooth contact has no friction.

Standard example: a uniform ladder of length 2a and weight W rests against a smooth vertical wall with its foot on rough ground (coefficient μ), at angle θ to the horizontal. Resolving: N = W and friction F = S (the wall reaction). Moments about the foot: S · 2a sin θ = W · a cos θ, so S = W/(2 tan θ). Equilibrium needs F ≤ μN, so tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ).

Exam tips: draw a clear diagram with every force labelled, state your origin and the order in r × F, and take moments about the point where the most unknown forces act.

notes.h: Newton's laws, momentum, angular momentum and energy
notes.body:
This topic sets up the general framework for particle dynamics. The laws hold in an inertial frame; position r(t), velocity v = ṙ and acceleration a = r̈ are vectors.

Newton's laws
- First law: a particle with no net force moves with constant velocity.
- Second law: F = dp/dt, where p = mv is the linear momentum; for constant mass this is F = ma.
- Third law: the forces two particles exert on each other are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and (strong form) along the line joining them.
- Impulse: ∫ F dt over a time interval equals the change in momentum. If the total external force on a system is zero, its total momentum is conserved.

Angular momentum
- About O: L = r × p = m r × v.
- dL/dt = v × mv + r × m v̇ = r × F = G, because v × v = 0. Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum.
- Central force (F parallel to r at all times): G = 0, so L is constant. Then r and v stay perpendicular to the fixed vector L, so the motion lies in a plane through O. This is the starting point for orbits.

Work and kinetic energy
- Kinetic energy T = ½ m|v|². Since d/dt(½ m v·v) = m v̇·v = F·v, the rate of working of F is F·v.
- Work done along a path C is W = ∫_C F·dr, and W = change in T (work–energy theorem).
- Example: a 2 kg particle whose velocity changes from (3, 0, 0) to (0, 4, 0) m/s gains ΔT = ½ × 2 × (16 − 9) = 7 J. The work depends only on speeds, not on the change in the velocity vector.

Conservative forces
- F is conservative if the work done between two points is independent of the path. Equivalently, F = −∇V for a potential energy V(r). On a simply connected region (for example all of ℝ³) a continuously differentiable F is conservative if and only if ∇ × F = 0.
- Then T + V = E is constant along the motion (energy conservation): dT/dt = F·v = −∇V·ṙ = −dV/dt.
- Standard potentials (z measured upwards): uniform gravity V = mgz; linear spring of stiffness k, V = ½ k x²; inverse-square attraction F = −(k/r²) r̂ with k > 0, V = −k/r.
- Test example: F = (2xy + z, x², x) has zero curl and equals −∇V with V = −(x²y + xz). F = (y, −x, 0) has curl (0, 0, −2), so it is not conservative.
- Non-conservative forces such as friction and air resistance do negative work, and then T + V decreases.

How the pieces fit together. Momentum conservation comes from zero net external force; angular momentum conservation from zero torque (central forces); energy conservation from conservative forces. Each gives a first integral that lowers the order of the equations, which is the main strategy for the rest of the module.

Exam tips: before using T + V = constant, say why the force is conservative (or check its curl); before using L = constant, say why the torque about your chosen point is zero.

notes.h: Particle motion with one degree of freedom
notes.body:
When a particle moves along a line (or its position is fixed by one coordinate), Newton's second law becomes a scalar ODE m ẍ = F. The aim is to extract as much as possible without fully solving it.

Force depending only on position: F = F(x)
- Define V(x) = −∫ F(x) dx, so F = −V′(x). Multiplying m ẍ = −V′(x) by ẋ and integrating gives the energy integral ½ m ẋ² + V(x) = E.
- Motion is possible only where V(x) ≤ E. Turning points (ẋ = 0) are where V(x) = E. Between two turning points the motion is a periodic oscillation.
- Time taken: t = ∫ dx / √(2(E − V(x))/m), choosing the sign of ẋ.
- Equilibria are points with V′(x₀) = 0. A minimum of V (V″(x₀) > 0) is stable; a maximum is unstable.
- Small oscillations about a stable equilibrium: put x = x₀ + ξ; then m ξ̈ ≈ −V″(x₀) ξ, simple harmonic motion with ω = √(V″(x₀)/m).
- Example: m = 1 and V = x³ − 3x. V′ = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; V″ = 6x. So x = 1 is stable with ω = √6, and x = −1 is unstable.

Escape speed. For radial motion under gravity, ẍ = −GM/x², so ½ ẋ² − GM/x is constant. To reach infinity from the surface (x = R) the speed must satisfy ½ v² ≥ GM/R, so v_esc = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) using g = GM/R². With g = 9.81 m/s² and R = 6.371 × 10⁶ m this is about 11.2 km/s.

Force depending on velocity: resisted motion
- Use m dv/dt = F(v) to find v(t), or m v dv/dx = F(v) to find v as a function of distance.
- Linear resistance, m dv/dt = −m k v: v = U e^(−kt).
- Quadratic resistance on a horizontal line, m dv/dt = −m k v²: v = U/(1 + kUt) in time. In distance, v dv/dx = −k v² gives v = U e^(−kx), so the speed halves after x = ln 2/k, at time t = 1/(kU).
- Falling with quadratic drag (x downwards): m dv/dt = mg − m k v². The terminal speed, where the acceleration vanishes, is √(g/k). With linear drag m dv/dt = mg − m k v the terminal speed is g/k.

Choosing the right form
- F(x) only: energy integral.
- F(v) only: separate variables in t or x.
- F(t) only: integrate twice.
- Mixed F(x, v): usually needs the methods of linear ODEs (for example the damped oscillator).

Exam tips: state your positive direction and make every force carry the right sign relative to it; check that resistance always opposes the velocity (for motion up and then down, you may need two separate equations).

Many problems are most cleanly written as one vector ODE, r̈ = f(r, ṙ, t), solved by integrating the vector directly or component by component.

Projectile without resistance (k a unit vector vertically upwards)
- r̈ = −g k with r(0) = 0 and ṙ(0) = u. Integrating twice: ṙ = u − g t k and r = u t − ½ g t² k.
- With speed u at angle α above the horizontal: x = u t cos α and z = u t sin α − ½ g t².
- Eliminating t gives the trajectory, a parabola: z = x tan α − g x²/(2u² cos² α).
- Time of flight on level ground: 2u sin α/g. Greatest height: u² sin² α/(2g). Range: R = u² sin 2α/g, largest when α = 45°, with maximum u²/g.
- Example: u = 20 m/s, α = 30°, g = 9.8 m/s² gives R = 400 sin 60°/9.8 ≈ 35.3 m and greatest height ≈ 5.10 m.
- Bounding parabola: the points reachable with launch speed u satisfy z ≤ u²/(2g) − g x²/(2u²). Write the trajectory as a quadratic in tan α and ask for real roots.

Projectile with linear resistance
- r̈ = −g k − λ ṙ (λ > 0, resistance per unit mass proportional to velocity).
- This is linear in ṙ: with integrating factor e^(λt), d/dt(e^(λt) ṙ) = −g e^(λt) k. So ṙ = (u + (g/λ)k) e^(−λt) − (g/λ)k.
- Integrating again with r(0) = 0: r = (1/λ)(u + (g/λ)k)(1 − e^(−λt)) − (g/λ) t k.
- As t → ∞, ṙ → −(g/λ)k (terminal velocity) and the horizontal displacement approaches u cos α/λ.
- The solution was checked against a numerical integration.

A three-dimensional example: charged particle in a magnetic field
- m r̈ = q ṙ × B with B = B k constant. Since the force is perpendicular to ṙ, the speed is constant (the force does no work).
- The k component gives ż constant. With ω = qB/m, the horizontal components satisfy u̇ = ω v and v̇ = −ω u (here u, v are the x and y velocity components). So u + iv = (u₀ + iv₀)e^(−iωt): uniform circular motion of radius m|v⊥|/(|q|B) in the horizontal plane.
- Combined with the constant ż, the path is a helix about the field direction.

Solving strategies for vector ODEs
- If the equation is linear with constant coefficients, look for an integrating factor or exponential solutions, exactly as for scalar ODEs.
- Take dot products with ṙ (for energy) or cross products with r (for angular momentum) to find first integrals.
- Use complex notation for rotation in a plane, as above.

Exam tips: state the direction of k and the sign of g in your equation; check limiting cases (for example, the resisted solution should reduce to r = u t − ½ g t² k as λ → 0, which you can confirm by expanding the exponential).

notes.h: Plane polar coordinates and central forces
notes.body:
For a force directed towards a fixed point, plane polar coordinates (r, θ) centred at that point are natural. This topic derives the polar form of acceleration and the u-equation for orbits.

Unit vectors and their derivatives
- e_r = (cos θ, sin θ), e_θ = (−sin θ, cos θ). These rotate with the particle.
- de_r/dt = θ̇ e_θ and de_θ/dt = −θ̇ e_r.

Velocity and acceleration (position r = r e_r)
- v = ṙ e_r + r θ̇ e_θ.
- a = (r̈ − r θ̇²) e_r + (r θ̈ + 2ṙ θ̇) e_θ.
- The transverse part can be written (1/r) d/dt(r² θ̇).
- The −r θ̇² term is the centripetal acceleration; 2ṙθ̇ is the Coriolis-type term. Both come from differentiating the rotating unit vectors.

Central forces. Let F = m f(r) e_r, with f(r) < 0 for attraction.
- Transverse equation: (1/r) d/dt(r² θ̇) = 0, so r² θ̇ = h is constant. h is the angular momentum per unit mass.
- Radial equation: r̈ − h²/r³ = f(r).
- Energy (if f is conservative, f = −dU/dr per unit mass): ½(ṙ² + h²/r²) + U(r) = E. The term h²/(2r²) acts like an extra repulsive potential, so the effective potential is U(r) + h²/(2r²).

The u-equation (Binet's equation). Put u = 1/r and use θ as the independent variable. Since θ̇ = h u²:
- ṙ = −(1/u²) u̇ = −h du/dθ.
- r̈ = −h (d²u/dθ²) θ̇ = −h² u² d²u/dθ².
- Substituting into the radial equation: d²u/dθ² + u = −f(1/u)/(h² u²).
This gives the orbit shape directly, or the force law from a known orbit.

Inverse-square attraction. f = −μ/r² = −μu² gives d²u/dθ² + u = μ/h², whose solution is u = (μ/h²)(1 + e cos(θ − θ₀)). This is a conic with the centre of force at a focus (next topic).

Finding a force law from an orbit. For r = 2a cos θ (a circle through the centre of force), u = sec θ/(2a). Then d²u/dθ² + u = sec³ θ/a = 8a² u³, so f = −h² u² × 8a²u³ = −8a²h²/r⁵: an attractive inverse fifth-power law.

Kepler's second law in this language: the rate at which the radius vector sweeps out area is dA/dt = ½ r² θ̇ = h/2, constant for any central force.

Exam tips: memorise the polar acceleration and be ready to derive it from the derivatives of e_r and e_θ; in the u-equation keep the factor h²u² on the force side, and check the sign convention for attraction.

Solving the u-equation for an inverse-square attraction gives conic orbits. This topic collects the geometry of conics and uses it to prove Kepler's three laws.

Polar equation of a conic (focus at the origin)
- l/r = 1 + e cos θ, with l > 0 the semi-latus rectum and e ≥ 0 the eccentricity (θ measured from the direction of closest approach).
- e = 0: circle. 0 < e < 1: ellipse. e = 1: parabola. e > 1: one branch of a hyperbola.
- For the orbit, l = h²/μ, where μ = GM (strictly G(M + m) for the two-body problem).

Ellipse facts (0 < e < 1)
- Closest and furthest distances: r_min = l/(1 + e) = a(1 − e) and r_max = l/(1 − e) = a(1 + e).
- Semi-major axis a = l/(1 − e²) = (r_min + r_max)/2. Semi-minor axis b = a√(1 − e²), and l = b²/a.
- Example: l = 6, e = 0.5 gives r_min = 4, r_max = 12, a = 8.

Energy and orbit type. At closest approach the speed is h/r_min, and a short calculation gives energy per unit mass E = −μ/(2a) for an ellipse. Hence:
- E < 0: ellipse (bound orbit). E = 0: parabola (just escapes). E > 0: hyperbola.
- Vis-viva equation for an ellipse: v² = μ(2/r − 1/a).

Kepler's laws
1. Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one focus. This follows from the inverse-square u-equation (bound orbits have E < 0).
2. The radius vector sweeps out equal areas in equal times. True for any central force: dA/dt = h/2.
3. The square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. Proof: the area πab is swept at rate h/2, so T = 2πab/h. With h² = μl = μb²/a, T = 2πab/(b√(μ/a)) = 2π a^(3/2)/√μ, so T² = 4π² a³/μ.

Examples
- In years and astronomical units (Sun-centred orbits) T² = a³, so an orbit with a = 4 AU has period 8 years.
- Geostationary orbit: with μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³ s⁻² and T = one sidereal day (86 164 s), a = (μT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 42 160 km from the Earth's centre.
- Perihelion data: if μ = 1 and the particle is at r = 1 with transverse speed 1.2, then h = 1.2, l = 1.44, e = l/r_min − 1 = 0.44, a = 1.44/(1 − 0.44²) ≈ 1.786, and T = 2π a^(3/2) ≈ 15.0 (checked by numerical integration).

Exam tips: always find h first (from position and transverse velocity), then l = h²/μ, then e from a known point; use E = −μ/(2a) as a quick check on a.

A steady motion is stable if small disturbances stay small. In this module the main case is a circular orbit under a central force: is a slightly disturbed circular orbit still nearly circular?

One-dimensional warm-up. For ẍ = g(x) with an equilibrium x₀ (g(x₀) = 0), put x = x₀ + ξ with ξ small. Then ξ̈ ≈ g′(x₀)ξ.
- g′(x₀) < 0: simple harmonic oscillation with ω² = −g′(x₀); stable.
- g′(x₀) > 0: exponential growth; unstable.
For a potential V this is the familiar "minimum of V is stable".

Circular orbits. Let the attraction per unit mass be F(r) > 0, so the radial equation is r̈ − h²/r³ = −F(r).
- A circular orbit of radius r₀ needs h²/r₀³ = F(r₀); its angular velocity is Ω with Ω² = F(r₀)/r₀.
- Keep h fixed and put r = r₀ + x. Expanding to first order:
  ẍ = h²/(r₀ + x)³ − F(r₀ + x) ≈ −[3h²/r₀⁴ + F′(r₀)] x = −[3F(r₀)/r₀ + F′(r₀)] x.
- So the orbit is stable when 3F(r₀)/r₀ + F′(r₀) > 0, and then the radius oscillates with ω_r² = 3F(r₀)/r₀ + F′(r₀).

Equivalent view via the effective potential U_eff(r) = h²/(2r²) + U(r) with U′ = F. Circular orbits are stationary points of U_eff, and U_eff″(r₀) = 3h²/r₀⁴ + F′(r₀), so stability is the condition that r₀ is a minimum of U_eff.

Power laws. For F = k/rⁿ (k > 0), F′ = −nk/rⁿ⁺¹ and
3F/r₀ + F′ = (3 − n)k/r₀ⁿ⁺¹.
- Circular orbits are stable if and only if n < 3.
- The ratio of radial to orbital frequency is ω_r/Ω = √(3 − n).
- The radius goes from a maximum to the next minimum while θ advances by the apsidal angle π/√(3 − n).

Checks against known cases
- Inverse square (n = 2): ω_r = Ω and the apsidal angle is π, so nearly circular orbits close after one revolution. These are Kepler ellipses.
- Linear (Hooke) attraction F = kr (n = −1): ω_r = 2Ω and the apsidal angle is π/2; the orbits are ellipses centred on the origin.
- Inverse cube (n = 3): the restoring term vanishes, so a small radial disturbance makes r drift steadily away and the orbit spirals in or out; the circular orbit is not stable.

Why it matters. Stability links back to the energy method for one degree of freedom: once h is fixed, the radial motion is a one-dimensional problem in U_eff. The same "linearise and check the sign" method is used for equilibria of rigid bodies and later for phase plane analysis.

Exam tips: compare the disturbed orbit with the circular orbit that has the same h (the disturbed orbit's h is conserved, and for a purely radial kick it equals the original h); expand (r₀ + x)⁻³ ≈ r₀⁻³(1 − 3x/r₀) carefully, and quote the condition in the form 3F/r₀ + F′ > 0 before specialising.

Problems with an axis of symmetry (bead on a rotating wire, particle on a cone or cylinder, motion in a uniform magnetic field) are handled in cylindrical polar coordinates (R, φ, z), with z along the axis.

Kinematics. With position r = R e_R + z k:
- v = Ṙ e_R + R φ̇ e_φ + ż k.
- a = (R̈ − R φ̇²) e_R + (R φ̈ + 2Ṙ φ̇) e_φ + z̈ k.
This is the plane polar result plus a z-component. If the force has no e_φ component, (1/R) d/dt(R²φ̇) = 0, so R²φ̇ (angular momentum per unit mass about the axis) is conserved.

Conical pendulum. A particle on a light string of length l moves in a horizontal circle with the string at a fixed angle α to the downward vertical. The radius is R = l sin α.
- Vertical: T cos α = mg. Radial: T sin α = m R ω² = m l sin α ω².
- Dividing: ω² = g/(l cos α). Example: l = 0.5 m, α = 60°, g = 9.8 m/s² gives ω² = 39.2 and ω ≈ 6.26 rad/s.

Particle on the smooth inside of a cone. The axis is vertical with the vertex downwards and semi-vertical angle α. The particle moves in a horizontal circle of radius R. The normal reaction N is perpendicular to the surface, with an inward horizontal component N cos α and an upward component N sin α.
- Vertical: N sin α = mg. Radial: N cos α = m v²/R.
- So v² = gR cot α. Higher circles need higher speeds.

Bead on a rotating wire. A smooth straight wire rotates in a horizontal plane about a vertical axis through one end with constant angular velocity ω. A bead starts at rest relative to the wire at distance a.
- Along the wire (radial): R̈ − R ω² = 0, since a smooth wire exerts no force along itself.
- With R(0) = a and Ṙ(0) = 0: R = a cosh ωt. The bead moves outwards even though nothing pushes it along the wire; in the rotating picture this is the "centrifugal" effect.
- Transverse: the wire supplies the force N = m(Rφ̈ + 2Ṙφ̇) = 2mṘω = 2maω² sinh ωt.
- Vertically the wire also supports the weight, giving a separate vertical reaction of size mg.

Motion on the smooth inner surface of a vertical cylinder of radius a. Then R = a and Ṙ = 0, so the radial equation gives the inward normal reaction N = m a φ̇² (the wall can push inwards because the particle is on the inside). With gravity only, the φ and z equations decouple: φ̇ is constant and z̈ = −g. So the particle goes round at a steady rate while falling freely, and the height is a quadratic function of the angle turned.

Charged particle in a uniform magnetic field along k: the motion is a helix about a line parallel to k (see the vector ODE topic). In cylindrical coordinates about that line, R is constant and φ̇ = −qB/m.

Exam tips: resolve along e_R, e_φ and k, list every force (including normal reactions in both perpendicular directions), and check the sign of the centripetal term −Rφ̇².

F = ma assumes a fixed body. Rockets, raindrops and chains gain or lose mass, and then you must apply Newton's second law to the whole system, including the bit of mass being transferred.

Derivation. A body has mass m(t) and velocity v(t). In a short time δt it gains mass δm (δm < 0 if it loses mass). The transferred mass moves with absolute velocity w just before joining (or just after leaving). An external force F acts.
- Momentum at time t: m v + δm w (for gain), or m v for loss with the lost part leaving at w afterwards. Either way the change in total momentum over δt is (m + δm)(v + δv) − m v − δm w.
- Setting this equal to F δt and letting δt → 0:
  m dv/dt = F + (w − v) dm/dt.
- Write u = w − v for the velocity of the transferred mass relative to the body. Then m dv/dt = F + u dm/dt.
- Equivalently d(mv)/dt = F + w dm/dt. Note that d(mv)/dt = F holds only if the transferred mass is at rest (w = 0).

Rockets. Exhaust leaves at speed c relative to the rocket, backwards, so u = −c (taking forwards positive) and dm/dt < 0.
- m dv/dt = −c dm/dt + F. The thrust is c|dm/dt|.
- In free space (F = 0): dv = −c dm/m, so v − v₀ = c ln(m₀/m) (Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation).
- Example: c = 3000 m/s, burning from 1000 kg to 250 kg: Δv = 3000 ln 4 ≈ 4159 m/s.
- Vertical launch in uniform gravity with constant burn rate k (m = m₀ − kt): m dv/dt = ck − mg, so v = c ln(m₀/(m₀ − kt)) − g t. The rocket leaves the ground only if the initial thrust exceeds the weight: ck > m₀g.

Accretion: a raindrop falling through stationary mist. Here w = 0, so d(mv)/dt = mg (downwards positive). If the mass grows linearly from zero, m = kt, then mv = ∫ kgt dt = kgt²/2, so v = gt/2: the drop accelerates at g/2, not g, because momentum is spent bringing the mist up to speed.

Points to watch
- Energy is usually not conserved in mass-transfer problems: picking up mass at rest is like a perfectly inelastic collision.
- Always identify which velocity is given (absolute or relative to the body) before using the equation.
- For chains falling off tables or being lifted, consider the moving part as the variable-mass body and treat the links joining it as the transferred mass, usually with w = 0.

Exam tips: derive the equation from momentum over a short interval if asked, rather than quoting F = d(mv)/dt; state your positive direction and the sign of dm/dt; check the free-space rocket case reduces to Tsiolkovsky.

cards.f: Moment of F (acting at r) about O
cards.b: G = r × F; magnitude |F| × perpendicular distance from O to the line of action.

cards.f: Moment about A in terms of the moment about O
cards.b: G_A = G_O − a × R, where a is the position of A and R the resultant force.

cards.f: Couple
cards.b: Two equal and opposite forces with different parallel lines of action; zero resultant, moment (r₁ − r₂) × F, the same about every point.

cards.f: Conditions for equilibrium of a rigid body
cards.b: Resultant force zero and total moment about any one point zero.

cards.f: Friction law at a rough contact
cards.b: |F| ≤ μN, with equality in limiting equilibrium.

cards.f: Ladder (smooth wall, rough floor μ, angle θ to horizontal)
cards.b: Equilibrium requires tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ) (uniform ladder).

cards.f: Effect of sliding a force along its line of action
cards.b: No change in its moment, since (r + sF) × F = r × F.

cards.f: Newton's second law in momentum form
cards.b: F = dp/dt with p = mv (inertial frame).

cards.f: Rate of change of angular momentum
cards.b: dL/dt = r × F, where L = r × mv, because v × v = 0.

cards.f: Why central-force motion is planar
cards.b: L = r × mv is constant, and r, v are always perpendicular to the fixed vector L.

cards.f: Work–energy theorem
cards.b: Work done ∫ F·dr equals the change in kinetic energy ½m|v|².

cards.f: Conservative force
cards.b: Work is path-independent; equivalently F = −∇V; on a simply connected region, ∇ × F = 0.

cards.f: Potential energy for inverse-square attraction k/r²
cards.b: V = −k/r.

cards.f: When is T + V constant?
cards.b: When all forces doing work are conservative (no friction or resistance).

cards.f: Energy integral for m ẍ = F(x)
cards.b: ½ m ẋ² + V(x) = E, where V = −∫F dx.

cards.f: Turning points
cards.b: Points where V(x) = E (so ẋ = 0); motion is restricted to V(x) ≤ E.

cards.f: Small-oscillation frequency about a minimum x₀ of V
Escape speed from a planet
cards.b: √(2GM/R) = √(2gR); about 11.2 km/s for the Earth.

cards.f: Speed vs distance for v̇ = −kv²
cards.b: v = U e^(−kx); speed halves after distance ln 2/k.

cards.f: Terminal speed, quadratic drag m v̇ = mg − mkv²
Which form for a velocity-dependent force?
cards.b: m dv/dt = F(v) for time; m v dv/dx = F(v) for distance.

cards.f: Range on level ground
cards.b: u² sin 2α/g; maximum u²/g at α = 45°.

cards.f: Trajectory equation of a projectile
cards.b: z = x tan α − g x²/(2u² cos² α).

cards.f: Greatest height of a projectile
cards.b: u² sin² α/(2g).

cards.f: Velocity with linear resistance r̈ = −gk − λṙ
cards.b: ṙ = (u + (g/λ)k)e^(−λt) − (g/λ)k; tends to −(g/λ)k.

cards.f: Bounding parabola for launch speed u
cards.b: z = u²/(2g) − g x²/(2u²).

cards.f: Charged particle in uniform B: path
cards.b: A helix along B; circular part has angular frequency |q|B/m, and the speed is constant.

cards.f: Velocity in plane polars
cards.b: v = ṙ e_r + r θ̇ e_θ.

cards.f: Acceleration in plane polars
cards.b: (r̈ − rθ̇²) e_r + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) e_θ, with transverse part (1/r) d/dt(r²θ̇).

cards.f: Derivatives of e_r and e_θ
cards.b: ė_r = θ̇ e_θ, ė_θ = −θ̇ e_r.

cards.f: Conserved quantity for any central force
cards.b: h = r²θ̇ (angular momentum per unit mass).

cards.f: u-equation for F = m f(r) e_r
cards.b: d²u/dθ² + u = −f(1/u)/(h²u²), with u = 1/r.

cards.f: ṙ in terms of u
cards.b: ṙ = −h du/dθ.

cards.f: Force law for orbit r = 2a cos θ
cards.b: Attractive, proportional to 1/r⁵ (f = −8a²h²/r⁵).

cards.f: Polar equation of a conic (focus at O)
cards.b: l/r = 1 + e cos θ; e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola.

cards.f: Semi-latus rectum for an inverse-square orbit
cards.b: l = h²/μ.

cards.f: Perihelion and aphelion distances
cards.b: a(1 − e) and a(1 + e), where a = l/(1 − e²).

cards.f: Energy of an elliptic orbit
cards.b: E = −μ/(2a) per unit mass.

cards.f: Kepler's third law (formula)
cards.b: T² = 4π²a³/μ.

cards.f: Kepler's second law: rate of sweeping area
cards.b: dA/dt = h/2, constant for any central force.

cards.f: Vis-viva equation
Condition for a stable circular orbit (attraction F(r) per unit mass)
cards.b: 3F(r₀)/r₀ + F′(r₀) > 0.

cards.f: Power-law attraction k/rⁿ: stable circular orbits iff
Radial vs orbital frequency for F ∝ r^(−n)
Apsidal angle for nearly circular orbits
cards.b: π/√(3 − n); π for inverse square, π/2 for Hooke's law.

cards.f: Effective potential
cards.b: U_eff(r) = h²/(2r²) + U(r); stable circular orbits are its minima.

cards.f: Stability of ẍ = g(x) at equilibrium x₀
cards.b: Stable (oscillatory) if g′(x₀) < 0; unstable if g′(x₀) > 0.

cards.f: Acceleration in cylindrical polars
cards.b: (R̈ − Rφ̇²) e_R + (Rφ̈ + 2Ṙφ̇) e_φ + z̈ k.

cards.f: Conical pendulum angular speed
cards.b: ω² = g/(l cos α), α measured from the vertical.

cards.f: Bead on a smooth rotating wire (from rest at R = a)
cards.b: R = a cosh ωt.

cards.f: Transverse force on the bead from the wire
cards.b: 2mṘω = 2maω² sinh ωt.

cards.f: Speed on the smooth inside of a cone (vertex down, semi-angle α)
cards.b: v² = gR cot α.

cards.f: Conserved quantity if the force has no e_φ component
cards.b: R²φ̇ (angular momentum about the axis).

cards.f: Equation of motion with mass transfer
cards.b: m dv/dt = F + u dm/dt, u = velocity of transferred mass relative to the body.

cards.f: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation
cards.b: Δv = c ln(m₀/m) in free space, c = exhaust speed relative to the rocket.

cards.f: Rocket thrust
cards.b: c|dm/dt|.

cards.f: When is d(mv)/dt = F correct?
cards.b: Only when the gained or lost mass is at rest (absolute velocity zero).

cards.f: Raindrop gaining stationary mist, m ∝ t, from rest
cards.b: Acceleration g/2.

cards.f: Lift-off condition, vertical rocket
cards.b: Initial thrust ck must exceed weight m₀g.

questions.q: A force F = (2, −1, 3) N acts at the point r = (1, 1, 0) m. What is its moment about the origin?
questions.why: G = r × F = (1·3 − 0·(−1), 0·2 − 1·3, 1·(−1) − 1·2) = (3, −3, −3). The vector (−3, 3, 3) is F × r, the cross product taken in the wrong order. (3, 3, −3) comes from forgetting the minus sign on the j cofactor when expanding the determinant. (2, −1, 0) multiplies matching components, which is not a cross product at all.

questions.q: Forces (0, 5, 0) N at (2, 0, 0) m and (0, −5, 0) N at (−2, 0, 0) m act on a body. What is their total moment about the point (1, 1, 0)?
questions.why: The forces form a couple, whose moment is the same about every point: (r₁ − r₂) × F = (4, 0, 0) × (0, 5, 0) = (0, 0, 20). Zero assumes that because the forces cancel, their moments cancel too, which is false when the lines of action differ. (0, 0, 10) is the moment of just one force about the origin. (0, 0, −20) takes the cross products in the order F × r.

questions.q: A uniform ladder of length 2a and weight W rests with its foot on rough horizontal ground (coefficient of friction μ) and its top against a smooth vertical wall, making angle θ with the horizontal. Show that equilibrium is possible only if tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ).
markScheme: Diagram with W at the midpoint, normal reaction N and friction F at the foot, horizontal reaction S at the wall
Resolves: N = W, F = S
Moments about the foot: S·2a sin θ = W·a cos θ
F = W/(2 tan θ)
Uses F ≤ μN to obtain tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ)
questions.modelAnswer: Forces: weight W at the midpoint; at the foot, normal reaction N upwards and friction F towards the wall; at the top, a horizontal reaction S away from the wall (no friction, since the wall is smooth). Resolving vertically, N = W; horizontally, F = S. Taking moments about the foot (removing N and F): S × 2a sin θ = W × a cos θ, so S = W cos θ/(2 sin θ) = W/(2 tan θ). Hence F = W/(2 tan θ). For equilibrium, F ≤ μN = μW, so W/(2 tan θ) ≤ μW, giving tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ).

questions.q: Which force field is conservative on ℝ³?
questions.why: (2xy + z, x², x) has zero curl and equals −∇V with V = −(x²y + xz). (yz, xz, 0) looks like part of ∇(xyz) but lacks the z-component xy; its curl is (−x, y, 0). (y, −x, 0) is a rotational field with curl (0, 0, −2). (x², y², xy) has first two components that are gradients, but the xy z-component spoils it: the curl is (x, −y, 0).

questions.q: A particle of mass 2 kg has its velocity changed from (3, 0, 0) m/s to (0, 4, 0) m/s. How much work was done on it?
questions.why: Work equals the change in kinetic energy: ½ × 2 × (4² − 3²) = 7 J. 25 J uses the magnitude of the change in velocity, |(−3, 4, 0)| = 5, but kinetic energy depends on speeds, not on the velocity change. 14 J omits the factor ½. 1 J subtracts the speeds before squaring, ½ × 2 × (4 − 3)².

questions.q: Show that the angular momentum L = r × mv of a particle about O satisfies dL/dt = r × F. Deduce that a particle moving under a central force about O moves in a plane through O.
markScheme: Differentiates the product: dL/dt = ṙ × mv + r × m v̇
ṙ × mv = 0 since ṙ = v
Uses F = m v̇ to get r × F
Central force: F parallel to r, so r × F = 0 and L is constant
r·L = 0 for all t, so r lies in the fixed plane through O perpendicular to L (if L ≠ 0)
questions.modelAnswer: dL/dt = d/dt(r × mv) = ṙ × mv + r × m v̇ (constant mass). The first term is v × mv = 0. Newton's second law gives m v̇ = F, so dL/dt = r × F. For a central force, F is parallel to r, so r × F = 0 and L is constant. Since L = r × mv, r·L = 0 at every time, so r always lies in the plane through O perpendicular to the fixed vector L (if L = 0 the motion is along a fixed line through O, which also lies in a plane). Hence the motion is planar.

questions.q: A particle of unit mass moves on a line with potential energy V(x) = x³ − 3x. Which statement about its equilibria is correct?
options: x = −1 is stable, since V has a maximum there
x = 1 is stable, with small-oscillation angular frequency 6
Both x = 1 and x = −1 are stable, since V′(±1) = 0
x = 1 is stable, with small-oscillation angular frequency √6
questions.why: V′ = 3x² − 3 vanishes at x = ±1 and V″ = 6x. At x = 1, V″ = 6 > 0 (a minimum), so it is stable with ω = √(V″/m) = √6. Choosing x = −1 confuses a maximum of V with a stable point; maxima are unstable. Frequency 6 forgets the square root in ω = √(V″/m). V′ = 0 only says both points are equilibria; stability depends on the sign of V″.

questions.q: A particle moves along a horizontal line with retardation k v² per unit mass, starting with speed U. How far does it travel before its speed is U/2?
questions.why: v dv/dx = −k v² gives dv/v = −k dx, so v = U e^(−kx) and v = U/2 when x = ln 2/k. 1/(kU) is the time to halve the speed (from v = U/(1 + kUt)), not the distance. 3/(8k) treats the deceleration as constant at its initial value kU². U/(2k) solves the problem as if the resistance were proportional to v (then v = U − kx).

questions.q: A particle is projected vertically upwards from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R (no atmosphere). Using an energy argument, find the least speed needed for it to escape to infinity, and express it in terms of g = GM/R².
markScheme: Equation ẍ = −GM/x² (x = distance from centre)
Energy integral ½ẋ² − GM/x = constant
Escape requires ẋ² ≥ 0 as x → ∞, so ½v² − GM/R ≥ 0
v_esc = √(2GM/R)
questions.modelAnswer: Let x be the distance from the planet's centre. Newton's law of gravitation gives ẍ = −GM/x². Multiplying by ẋ and integrating: ½ẋ² − GM/x = ½v² − GM/R, where v is the launch speed. As x → ∞ the left side tends to ½ẋ², which must be ≥ 0 if the particle never turns back. So we need ½v² ≥ GM/R, that is v ≥ √(2GM/R). With GM = gR², the escape speed is √(2gR) (about 11.2 km/s for the Earth).

questions.q: A projectile is launched from level ground at 20 m/s, 30° above the horizontal (g = 9.8 m/s², no air resistance). What is its range on the ground?
questions.why: R = u² sin 2α/g = 400 × sin 60°/9.8 ≈ 35.3 m. 20.4 m uses sin α instead of sin 2α. 5.10 m is the greatest height u² sin² α/(2g), not the range. 17.7 m is half the range, from using the time to the highest point as the time of flight.

questions.q: A particle moves under r̈ = −g k − λṙ (k upwards, λ > 0). What does its velocity tend to as t → ∞?
options: u − (g/λ)k, where u is the initial velocity
questions.why: ṙ = (u + (g/λ)k)e^(−λt) − (g/λ)k, and the exponential term decays, leaving the terminal velocity −(g/λ)k, where drag balances gravity. Zero would mean resistance stops the particle completely, but gravity keeps acting. −(λ/g)k inverts the ratio (check the units: g/λ is a speed). u − (g/λ)k forgets that the initial velocity decays like e^(−λt).

questions.q: A particle is projected from the origin with speed u at angle α above the horizontal, under gravity only. Derive the equation of its path and show that its range on the horizontal plane through the origin is u² sin 2α/g. For what α is the range greatest?
markScheme: Integrates r̈ = −gk to x = ut cos α, z = ut sin α − ½gt²
Eliminates t: z = x tan α − gx²/(2u²cos²α)
Sets z = 0, x ≠ 0: x = 2u² sin α cos α/g
= u² sin 2α/g
Greatest when sin 2α = 1, α = 45°, range u²/g
questions.modelAnswer: With k upwards, r̈ = −gk. Integrating with ṙ(0) = (u cos α, u sin α) and r(0) = 0 gives x = ut cos α and z = ut sin α − ½gt². Then t = x/(u cos α), so z = x tan α − gx²/(2u² cos² α), a parabola. Setting z = 0 with x ≠ 0: tan α = gx/(2u² cos² α), so x = 2u² sin α cos α/g = u² sin 2α/g. For fixed u this is largest when sin 2α = 1, that is α = 45°, giving range u²/g.

questions.q: In plane polar coordinates, what is the radial component of acceleration?
questions.why: Differentiating v = ṙ e_r + rθ̇ e_θ and using ė_θ = −θ̇ e_r gives radial part r̈ − rθ̇². With a plus sign, the centripetal term points the wrong way: uniform circular motion has acceleration rθ̇² towards the centre. r̈ alone forgets that e_r and e_θ rotate. rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇ is the transverse component.

questions.q: A particle moves under a central force with constant h = r²θ̇ along the orbit r = 2a cos θ (a circle through the centre of force). How does the force depend on r?
questions.why: With u = sec θ/(2a), d²u/dθ² + u = sec³ θ/a = 8a²u³, and f = −h²u²(u″ + u) = −8a²h²u⁵, an inverse fifth-power attraction. Inverse square assumes every closed orbit is a Kepler ellipse with the centre at a focus. Inverse cube comes from forgetting the factor h²u² in front of (u″ + u). A force proportional to r gives ellipses centred on the force centre, but here the centre of force lies on the circle itself.

questions.q: Starting from r = r e_r with e_r = (cos θ, sin θ) and e_θ = (−sin θ, cos θ), derive the polar expressions for velocity and acceleration. Hence show that for a central force r²θ̇ is constant.
markScheme: ė_r = θ̇ e_θ and ė_θ = −θ̇ e_r
v = ṙ e_r + rθ̇ e_θ
a = (r̈ − rθ̇²)e_r + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇)e_θ
Transverse part = (1/r) d/dt(r²θ̇)
Central force has no e_θ component, so r²θ̇ = constant
questions.modelAnswer: Differentiating e_r = (cos θ, sin θ) gives θ̇(−sin θ, cos θ) = θ̇ e_θ; similarly ė_θ = θ̇(−cos θ, −sin θ) = −θ̇ e_r. Then v = d/dt(r e_r) = ṙ e_r + r θ̇ e_θ. Differentiating again: a = r̈ e_r + ṙθ̇ e_θ + (ṙθ̇ + rθ̈) e_θ + rθ̇(−θ̇ e_r) = (r̈ − rθ̇²) e_r + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) e_θ. The transverse part equals (1/r) d/dt(r²θ̇), since d/dt(r²θ̇) = 2rṙθ̇ + r²θ̈. For a central force F = F(r) e_r, the e_θ equation is m(1/r) d/dt(r²θ̇) = 0, so r²θ̇ is constant.

questions.q: An orbit has polar equation 6/r = 1 + 0.5 cos θ. What is its semi-major axis?
questions.why: a = l/(1 − e²) = 6/0.75 = 8, equivalently the mean of r_min = 4 and r_max = 12. 12 is the furthest distance l/(1 − e), not the semi-major axis. 4 is the closest distance l/(1 + e). 6 is the semi-latus rectum l, which equals a only for a circle.

questions.q: A planet orbits the Sun with semi-major axis 4 AU. Using Kepler's third law (period 1 year at 1 AU), what is its period?
questions.why: T² ∝ a³, so T = 4^(3/2) = 8 years. 16 years assumes T ∝ a². 64 years gives a³ itself, forgetting to take the square root. 2 years assumes T ∝ √a.

questions.q: Using Kepler's second law and the properties of the ellipse, prove Kepler's third law T² = 4π²a³/μ for a particle in an elliptic orbit under the attraction μ/r² per unit mass.
markScheme: Areal rate dA/dt = ½r²θ̇ = h/2
Area of ellipse πab, so T = 2πab/h
Orbit equation gives l = h²/μ
Ellipse geometry: l = b²/a
Substitutes to get T = 2πa^(3/2)/√μ, so T² = 4π²a³/μ
questions.modelAnswer: In time dt the radius vector sweeps area ½r²dθ, so dA/dt = ½r²θ̇ = h/2, which is constant. One orbit sweeps the whole ellipse, area πab, so T = πab/(h/2) = 2πab/h. From the u-equation for inverse-square attraction, the orbit is l/r = 1 + e cos θ with l = h²/μ, so h = √(μl). For an ellipse l = b²/a, so h = b√(μ/a). Then T = 2πab/(b√(μ/a)) = 2πa^(3/2)/√μ, and squaring gives T² = 4π²a³/μ.

questions.q: For an attractive central force of magnitude k/rⁿ per unit mass (k > 0), when are circular orbits stable?
questions.why: The condition 3F/r₀ + F′(r₀) > 0 becomes (3 − n)k/r₀ⁿ⁺¹ > 0, so n < 3. 'n > 3' reverses the inequality. 'n < 2' wrongly treats the inverse square as the borderline case; the borderline is the inverse cube. 'Only n = 2' confuses stability with closed orbits: inverse square gives closed orbits, but circular orbits are stable for every n < 3.

questions.q: A particle moves under an attraction k r per unit mass (k > 0). For a nearly circular orbit with orbital angular velocity Ω, what is the angular frequency ω_r of the small radial oscillations?
questions.why: ω_r² = 3F/r₀ + F′(r₀) = 3k + k = 4k, and Ω² = F/r₀ = k, so ω_r = 2Ω (apsidal angle π/2, ellipses centred on O). Ω is the inverse-square result. √2 Ω comes from using n = 1 in √(3 − n), but F ∝ r means n = −1. √3 Ω keeps 3F/r₀ and forgets the F′(r₀) term.

questions.q: A particle moves under an attractive central force F(r) per unit mass, with angular momentum per unit mass h. Show that a circular orbit of radius r₀ exists if h² = r₀³F(r₀), and that it is stable to small radial disturbances (with h fixed) if 3F(r₀)/r₀ + F′(r₀) > 0.
markScheme: Radial equation r̈ − h²/r³ = −F(r)
Circular orbit r̈ = 0: h² = r₀³F(r₀)
Puts r = r₀ + x and expands (r₀ + x)⁻³ ≈ r₀⁻³(1 − 3x/r₀), F(r₀ + x) ≈ F(r₀) + xF′(r₀)
Obtains ẍ = −(3h²/r₀⁴ + F′(r₀))x = −(3F(r₀)/r₀ + F′(r₀))x
SHM (stable) when the bracket is positive
questions.modelAnswer: The radial equation is r̈ − h²/r³ = −F(r). A circular orbit has r = r₀ constant, so h²/r₀³ = F(r₀), that is h² = r₀³F(r₀). Now let r = r₀ + x with x small and h unchanged. Then (r₀ + x)⁻³ ≈ r₀⁻³(1 − 3x/r₀) and F(r₀ + x) ≈ F(r₀) + xF′(r₀). Substituting, ẍ ≈ h²/r₀³ − 3h²x/r₀⁴ − F(r₀) − xF′(r₀) = −(3h²/r₀⁴ + F′(r₀))x, using h²/r₀³ = F(r₀). Since h²/r₀⁴ = F(r₀)/r₀, this is ẍ = −(3F(r₀)/r₀ + F′(r₀))x. If the bracket is positive, x performs simple harmonic motion and stays small, so the orbit is stable; if it is negative, x grows exponentially.

questions.q: A smooth straight wire rotates in a horizontal plane about a vertical axis through one end with constant angular velocity ω. A bead starts at rest relative to the wire at distance a from the axis. What is its distance R(t) from the axis?
questions.why: Along the smooth wire there is no force, so R̈ − Rω² = 0, giving R = A cosh ωt + B sinh ωt; R(0) = a and Ṙ(0) = 0 give a cosh ωt. a cos ωt comes from the wrong sign of the centripetal term (R̈ + Rω² = 0). a e^(ωt) is a solution of the ODE but has Ṙ(0) = aω, so it violates the starting condition. A constant R assumes that no force along the wire means no motion along it, forgetting the −Rφ̇² term in the radial acceleration.

questions.q: A conical pendulum has string length 0.5 m and the string makes 60° with the vertical (g = 9.8 m/s²). What is its angular speed?
questions.why: T cos α = mg and T sin α = m(l sin α)ω² give ω² = g/(l cos α) = 9.8/0.25 = 39.2, so ω ≈ 6.26 rad/s. 4.76 rad/s swaps sin and cos when resolving (ω² = g/(l sin α)). 4.43 rad/s is √(g/l), the small-oscillation formula for a simple pendulum, which does not apply here. 5.83 rad/s uses the string length l instead of l sin α as the radius of the circle, giving ω² = g tan α/l.

questions.q: A smooth straight wire rotates in a horizontal plane about a vertical axis through one end O, with constant angular velocity ω. A bead of mass m is released from rest relative to the wire at distance a from O. Find its distance from O at time t and the horizontal force the wire exerts on it.
markScheme: Uses cylindrical/polar acceleration with φ̇ = ω, φ̈ = 0
Radial: m(R̈ − Rω²) = 0 (smooth wire)
R = a cosh ωt from R(0) = a, Ṙ(0) = 0
Transverse: N = m(Rφ̈ + 2Ṙφ̇) = 2mṘω
N = 2maω² sinh ωt (perpendicular to the wire, horizontal)
questions.modelAnswer: Use polar coordinates in the horizontal plane with φ̇ = ω and φ̈ = 0. The wire is smooth, so it exerts no force along itself: the radial equation is m(R̈ − Rω²) = 0, so R = A cosh ωt + B sinh ωt. R(0) = a gives A = a, and Ṙ(0) = 0 gives B = 0, so R = a cosh ωt. The horizontal force from the wire is perpendicular to it (the e_φ direction), of size N = m(Rφ̈ + 2Ṙφ̇) = 2mṘω = 2maω² sinh ωt. (The wire also provides a vertical reaction mg to support the weight.)

questions.q: A rocket in deep space has exhaust speed 3000 m/s relative to the rocket and burns fuel until its mass falls from 1000 kg to 250 kg. Starting from rest, what is its final speed?
questions.why: Tsiolkovsky: Δv = c ln(m₀/m) = 3000 ln 4 ≈ 4159 m/s. 2250 m/s treats the fuel as ejected in a single burst at 3000 m/s relative to the final rocket; burning continuously does better. 9000 m/s treats 3000 m/s as the fuel's absolute speed and balances 750 × 3000 against 250v. 863 m/s uses ln(1000/750), the ratio of initial mass to fuel mass instead of initial to final mass.

questions.q: A raindrop of mass m(t) falls with velocity v (downwards positive) through a cloud of stationary droplets, which it absorbs. Ignoring air resistance, which is its equation of motion?
questions.why: In m dv/dt = F + (w − v) dm/dt, the absorbed droplets have w = 0, giving m dv/dt = mg − v dm/dt, which is d(mv)/dt = mg. m dv/dt = mg ignores the momentum needed to bring the absorbed mass up to speed. m dv/dt = mg + v dm/dt has the transfer term with the wrong sign, as if the absorbed mass pushed the drop forwards. d(mv)/dt = mg − v dm/dt counts the momentum transfer twice: expanding it gives m dv/dt = mg − 2v dm/dt.

questions.q: A body of mass m(t) moving with velocity v gains mass at rate dm/dt; the mass gained has velocity w just before joining. An external force F acts. Derive m dv/dt = F + (w − v) dm/dt. Hence show that a rocket in free space whose exhaust leaves at speed c relative to it satisfies v − v₀ = c ln(m₀/m).
markScheme: Momentum before: mv + δm w
Momentum after: (m + δm)(v + δv)
Change = F δt; divides by δt, lets δt → 0, neglecting δm δv
m dv/dt = F + (w − v) dm/dt
Rocket: w − v = −c, F = 0: m dv/dt = −c dm/dt, integrate to v − v₀ = c ln(m₀/m)
questions.modelAnswer: Consider the system of the body plus the mass δm about to join it. At time t its momentum is mv + δm w. At t + δt the combined mass m + δm has velocity v + δv, momentum (m + δm)(v + δv). Newton's second law for the system: (m + δm)(v + δv) − mv − δm w = F δt + o(δt). Expanding and dropping the second-order term δm δv: m δv + (v − w)δm = F δt. Dividing by δt and letting δt → 0 gives m dv/dt = F + (w − v) dm/dt. (The same equation holds for mass loss, with dm/dt < 0 and w the velocity of the ejected mass.) For a rocket with exhaust moving backwards at speed c relative to it, w − v = −c, and in free space F = 0: m dv/dt = −c dm/dt. So dv = −c dm/m, and integrating from mass m₀ (speed v₀) to m gives v − v₀ = c ln(m₀/m).

questions.q:
A particle P moves under an attraction μ/r² per unit mass towards a fixed point O. Use plane polar coordinates (r, θ) centred on O, with h = r²θ̇.
(a) Show that u = 1/r satisfies d²u/dθ² + u = μ/h², and deduce that the orbit is a conic l/r = 1 + e cos θ with l = h²/μ. [7]
(b) Take μ = 1. At its closest approach P is at distance 1 from O with speed 1.2. Find h, l, e and the semi-major axis a, and show that the orbit is an ellipse. [6]
(c) Find the period of the orbit and the greatest distance of P from O. [4]
(d) Verify your value of a using the energy. [3]
markScheme: (a) ṙ = −h du/dθ and r̈ = −h²u² d²u/dθ²
(a) Substitutes in r̈ − rθ̇² = −μu² to get u″ + u = μ/h²
(a) General solution u = μ/h²(1 + e cos(θ − θ₀)), choose θ₀ = 0
(b) At closest approach the velocity is transverse: h = 1 × 1.2 = 1.2; l = 1.44
(b) r_min = l/(1 + e) gives e = 0.44 < 1, so ellipse; a = l/(1 − e²) ≈ 1.786
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) With u = 1/r and θ̇ = hu², ṙ = −u̇/u² = −(du/dθ)θ̇/u² = −h du/dθ, and r̈ = −h (d²u/dθ²)θ̇ = −h²u² d²u/dθ². Also rθ̇² = (1/u)h²u⁴ = h²u³. The radial equation r̈ − rθ̇² = −μ/r² = −μu² becomes −h²u²(u″ + u) = −μu², so d²u/dθ² + u = μ/h². This is a forced harmonic equation with general solution u = μ/h² + A cos(θ − θ₀). Writing A = eμ/h² (e ≥ 0) and measuring θ from closest approach (θ₀ = 0): 1/r = (μ/h²)(1 + e cos θ), that is l/r = 1 + e cos θ with l = h²/μ, a conic with O at a focus.

(b) At closest approach ṙ = 0, so the velocity is transverse and h = r × (speed) = 1 × 1.2 = 1.2. Then l = h²/μ = 1.44. At θ = 0, r_min = l/(1 + e) = 1, so e = 1.44 − 1 = 0.44. Since 0 ≤ e < 1, the orbit is an ellipse. a = l/(1 − e²) = 1.44/(1 − 0.1936) = 1.44/0.8064 ≈ 1.786 (exactly 25/14).

(c) Kepler's third law: T = 2πa^(3/2)/√μ = 2π(1.7857)^(1.5) ≈ 2π × 2.386 ≈ 15.0. The greatest distance is r_max = l/(1 − e) = 1.44/0.56 ≈ 2.571 (= 18/7). Check: r_min + r_max = 1 + 2.571 = 2a. (A numerical integration of the equations of motion gives the same period and r_max.)

(d) The energy per unit mass is E = ½v² − μ/r = ½(1.44) − 1 = −0.28 < 0, confirming a bound orbit. For an ellipse E = −μ/(2a), so a = 1/(2 × 0.28) = 1/0.56 ≈ 1.786, agreeing with (b).

questions.q:
A rocket of initial mass m₀ (including fuel) stands on the ground and is fired vertically upwards. It burns fuel at a constant rate k, and the exhaust leaves at speed c relative to the rocket. Take gravity g as constant and ignore air resistance.
(a) Derive the equation of motion while the fuel burns, explaining the sign of each term. [5]
(b) Show that the rocket leaves the ground immediately only if ck > m₀g, and find v(t). [5]
(c) Take m₀ = 1000 kg, k = 10 kg/s, c = 2000 m/s, g = 9.8 m/s² and suppose the fuel runs out when the mass is 400 kg. Find the burn time, the speed at burn-out and the height at burn-out. [10]
markScheme: (a) Applies m dv/dt = F + (w − v) dm/dt with dm/dt = −k, w − v = −c (upwards positive), F = −mg
(a) Gets (m₀ − kt) dv/dt = ck − (m₀ − kt)g, thrust ck up, weight down
(b) Initial acceleration ck/m₀ − g > 0 requires ck > m₀g
(b) v = c ln(m₀/(m₀ − kt)) − gt
(c) Height z = c[T − (m/k) ln(m₀/m)] − ½gT²
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Take upwards as positive. The mass is m = m₀ − kt, so dm/dt = −k. The exhaust moves downwards at speed c relative to the rocket, so its velocity relative to the rocket is w − v = −c. The external force is the weight −mg. The mass-transfer equation m dv/dt = F + (w − v) dm/dt gives m dv/dt = −mg + (−c)(−k) = ck − mg. The term ck is the thrust (upwards, because mass is thrown downwards) and mg is the weight.

(b) At t = 0, dv/dt = ck/m₀ − g, which is positive only if ck > m₀g; otherwise the ground reaction is needed and the rocket sits on the pad until enough fuel has burnt. Assuming ck > m₀g: dv/dt = ck/(m₀ − kt) − g. Integrating from v(0) = 0: v = −c ln(m₀ − kt) + c ln m₀ − gt = c ln(m₀/(m₀ − kt)) − gt.

(c) Here ck = 20 000 N > m₀g = 9800 N, so it lifts off at once. Fuel burnt 600 kg at 10 kg/s gives burn time T = 60 s. Speed at burn-out: v = 2000 ln(1000/400) − 9.8 × 60 = 2000 × 0.9163 − 588 ≈ 1832.6 − 588 ≈ 1245 m/s. Height: z = ∫₀ᵀ v dt. With s = 1 − kt/m₀, ∫₀ᵀ c ln(m₀/(m₀ − kt)) dt = (cm₀/k)[s ln s − s + 1] evaluated at s = 0.4, which equals c[T − (m/k) ln(m₀/m)] with m = 400 kg. This is 2000[60 − 40 ln 2.5] = 2000[60 − 36.65] ≈ 46 700 m. Subtract ½gT² = 0.5 × 9.8 × 3600 = 17 640 m, giving z ≈ 29 060 m, about 29.1 km. (A numerical integration gives 29 057 m.)
